title: Measuring and ratios in baking
examples: If I want to make a giant cake, how do I change the recipe?
What is the difference between using cups and weighing ingredients?
If the recipe calls for three parts flour to one part sugar, what does that mean?

explain.say: Today we learn about measuring things in baking.
We use a scale to weigh things by mass.
To scale a recipe means changing the amounts for different numbers of people.
Ratios compare amounts using a fixed relationship.
For example, a ratio of two parts flour to one part sugar means doubling the flour and sugar.
In real life, you use ratios when making juice.

draw.text: Juice: 3 parts juice to 1 part water

faq.q: Why is weighing better than using cups?
faq.a: Weighing gives a more accurate measurement because different ingredients can pack differently into a cup. You might ask if volume or mass is better.
asks: Is a cup always the same amount?
Should I use a scale or a cup?

faq.q: If I halve a recipe, do I just divide every number by two?
faq.a: Yes, you must divide every single ingredient amount by two to keep the ratios correct. Another way to ask is, what is half the recipe?
asks: How do I cut a recipe in half?
If I use half the ingredients, is it okay?

faq.q: What does a ratio of 2:1 actually mean for baking?
faq.a: It means for every two units of one ingredient, you must use one unit of the other. You could also ask what the proportion is, or how ingredients relate.
asks: What is the proportion of flour to sugar?
If the ratio is 3 to 1, how much do I need?

faq.q: Can I scale a recipe up by a quarter?
faq.a: Yes, you multiply every ingredient amount by one quarter. You might ask how to increase the recipe by 25 percent.
asks: How do I make this recipe bigger?
What if I want 12 servings instead of 6?

faq.q: Do I need to worry about different units when scaling?
faq.a: If the original recipe uses grams, keep using grams for the scaled version. Always check the units before multiplying or dividing. You might ask about unit consistency.
asks: If it says 1 cup, should I use grams?
Do I change units when I scale?

facts: Weighing ingredients by mass, like grams, is more accurate than using volume measures.
To scale a recipe, you multiply or divide all ingredient amounts by a consistent factor.
A ratio compares the relative amounts of two or more ingredients.
If a recipe ratio is 3:2, it means for every three parts of the first item, there are two parts of the second.

quiz.say: A recipe needs 300 grams of flour and 150 grams of sugar. If you want to use 600 grams of flour, what should the sugar be?
quiz.why: You multiplied the flour by two, so you must also multiply the sugar by two, making it 300 grams.

wrong.0: This is the original amount, but you changed the flour amount, so the sugar must change too.
wrong.1: This is adding the original amounts together, which does not keep the ratio correct.
wrong.2: This is multiplying the two original amounts together, which is not how ratios work.

quiz.say: A recipe calls for a ratio of 2 parts butter to 3 parts flour. If you use 100 grams of butter, how much flour do you need?
quiz.why: The ratio shows that flour is one and a half times the amount of butter, so 100 grams times one and a half is 150 grams.

wrong.0: This assumes the ratio is 1:1, ignoring the stated relationship.
wrong.2: This is simply doubling the butter amount, ignoring the ratio relationship.
wrong.3: This is dividing the butter amount by two, which is incorrect for this ratio.

quiz.say: To make a small batch of cookies, you need to scale a recipe from 12 servings down to 4 servings. What is the scaling factor?
quiz.why: You divide the new number of servings by the original number of servings, so 4 divided by 12 equals one third.

wrong.1: This is dividing 12 by 4, which gives the wrong direction for the factor.
wrong.2: This would be correct if you were scaling from 12 to 6 servings.
wrong.3: This is using the new serving number without dividing by the original amount.
